voiceover: Why does a soap bubble wear a rainbow—and why does it keep changing?
visual_direction: Large iridescent bubble on a deep navy background; slow push-in; transparent film, not a solid rainbow ball.

voiceover: Its skin is a thin film of soapy water.
visual_direction: Show a thin cross-section between air layers; label schematic, not to scale.

voiceover: When white light hits it, some reflects from the outer surface. The rest enters the film, bounces off the inner surface, and emerges beside the first reflection.
visual_direction: Animate one incoming white ray, a first reflected ray and a second ray that enters the film and returns.

voiceover: One reflection flips phase by half a cycle. The two waves overlap. Depending on film thickness and viewing angle, some wavelengths reinforce each other while others cancel.
visual_direction: Show a half-cycle phase inversion, then constructive and destructive sine-wave examples.
Display the term over a large bubble with coloured bands.

voiceover: Gravity drains liquid down the bubble, changing its thickness, so the colours shift across its surface.
visual_direction: Show liquid drainage arrow and spectral bands; viewing angle shown by a small eye/camera icon.

voiceover: Just before it bursts, extremely thin patches can look dark: reflected visible wavelengths cancel. The rainbow is made by light waves adding—and subtracting.
visual_direction: Show a small dark patch and two opposite-phase waves cancelling; end on the complete bubble.
